#### `On`

```java
public final class On
```

Exports a static method as an event handler: the Java face of the Rust SDK's `event!`. The server
has one event kind, `xdr-merge`, so there is one annotation, `XdrMerge`. The processor
generates the export that decodes the event into the method's parameters and the
`__udf_sig_<name>` export reading `event xdr-merge/1 ...`, which `event-set` checks
before binding. The parameter types are part of the kind, so a handler with another signature does not
compile. A handler returns a `Resolution`; an exception fails the call with its message.
```text
@On.XdrMerge("merge_counter")
static Resolution mergeCounter(EventRecord current, EventRecord incoming, Conflict conflict) {
...
return Resolution.record(out);
}
```
A handler may also take the raw form `int name(int args, int argc)`, exported as it is with only
the signature generated; it decodes the call with `Conflict#decode` and answers with the
`Conflict` verdict methods. The name is the method's when the annotation's value is empty.

#### `On.XdrMerge`

```java
public @interface XdrMerge
```

`(EventRecord current, EventRecord incoming, Conflict conflict)`; answers keep-local, take-remote,
policy, delete or record. The two records are `conflict.local` and `conflict.remote`.

#### `Resolution`

```java
public final class Resolution
```

What an `xdr-merge` handler returns: the Java face of the Rust SDK's `Resolution`. Keep the
current record, apply the incoming write whole, let the namespace's policy decide, remove the record, or
the final record.

```java
public static Resolution keepLocal()
```

Keep the local record; the incoming write is dropped.

#### `Resolution.takeRemote`

```java
public static Resolution takeRemote()
```

Apply the incoming write whole, as if it had won every bin.

#### `Resolution.policy`

```java
public static Resolution policy()
```

Let the namespace's policy decide, as it would have without the event.

#### `Resolution.delete`

```java
public static Resolution delete()
```

Remove the record on this cluster. The other cluster decides for itself, so a merge that deletes has
to delete on both sides for the two to agree. A record resolution with no bins left in it is not
this: it is the handler's failure.

#### `Resolution.record`

```java
public static Resolution record(MapBuilder bins)
```

The final record: these bins, whole - a bin not in the map, or set to nil, is deleted - keeping the
TTL the incoming write asked for.


As `record(MapBuilder)`, with a TTL in seconds: 0 for the namespace default.

#### `EventRecord`

```java
public final class EventRecord implements RecordReader
```

One record an event hands over: each side of a merge, the current record and the incoming write. It is
read-only, and it reads like the record of a call - the same readers, through
`RecordReader` - with what an event adds: the names of its bins, the bins this side deleted, and,
where the server keeps them, when and by whom each bin was last written.
A handler changes a record by answering with the bins it should have
(`Resolution#record`); `withBins` fills such an answer with every bin of this record the
handler did not decide.

#### `EventRecord.withBins`

```java
public MapBuilder withBins(MapBuilder overrides)
```

Puts every bin of this record that `overrides` lacks into it, by position, and returns it: for
a `record` answer that changes a few bins and keeps the rest. This prefers one side, so an
`xdr-merge` handler that uses it on the current record is not symmetric;
`Pair#withNewer` is the symmetric form.

#### `Conflict`

```java
public final class Conflict
```

What an `xdr-merge` event is about: the current record (`local`, read by index 0), the
incoming XDR write (`remote`, index 1), and the description. A handler must be pure and
convergent: both data centres merge the same pair with the sides swapped and must land on the same record.
`remoteNewer` orders a bin's two sides by its own LUT and then source id, which is symmetric;
"mine first" is not.

#### `Pair.withNewer`

```java
public MapBuilder withNewer(MapBuilder overrides)
```

Puts into `overrides` every bin either side has that it lacks, from the side that wrote the bin
later - which is what the policy would have kept - so a handler merges the bins it knows about and
leaves the rest as they would have been. Symmetric: both DCs order the two sides the same way.
Returns `overrides`.

#### `Both`

```java
public final class Both<T>
```

A bin on both sides of a conflict, either of which may be missing (null), with the merges a resolver
reaches for: the Java face of the Rust SDK's `Both<T>`. `Pair` builds one per bin.

#### `Both.remoteNewer`

```java

```

Whether the remote side wrote this bin later: by the bin's LUT where the server keeps one, the
record's otherwise, and on a tie by source id - the order the server's own bin convergence uses, so
"newer" means the same on both DCs even when the clocks agreed to the millisecond.
